title: Letters From Hash-Marked Codes
statement:
A message was encoded letter by letter. The letters a to i became the single digits 1 to 9. The letters j to z became the two-digit numbers 10 to 26 followed by a # mark.

You get the encoded string code, which is always a valid encoding. Return the original message.

examples.why: 3 is c and 1 is a. The 2 before "6#" is not its own letter: "26#" together is z.
Each # closes a two-digit code: 10 is j, 11 is k.
No # follows, so these are two separate single digits, not the code for l.

constraints: code has only digits and #, and is a valid encoding
hints: Reading left to right, how do you know whether a digit is a whole letter or the first half of a two-digit code?
Peek two characters ahead: if there is a # there, the current two digits form one code.
Or read from the right: a # means take the two digits before it; any other digit is a letter on its own. Reverse at the end.

explain.intuition:
A digit on its own is ambiguous: "26" could be b, f or the first part of z. The # mark removes the ambiguity, but it comes after the digits it belongs to. So either look ahead, or read the string backwards so the mark comes first.

Looking ahead: at position i, if code[i + 2] is #, the two digits at i and i + 1 form one letter and you jump by 3. Otherwise the single digit is a letter and you move by 1.
steps: If i + 2 < n and code[i + 2] === "#", decode code.slice(i, i + 2) and move i by 3.
Otherwise decode the single digit code[i] and move i by 1.
Map number k to the letter with code 96 + k. Join and return.
pitfalls: Greedily reading two digits whenever they form a number ≤ 26. Without a # they are separate letters, as in "12".
Building the output with repeated string concatenation in a language where that is quadratic.

solutions.title: Look two ahead
solutions.idea: A # two places ahead means the next two digits are one code; otherwise one digit is one letter.

solutions.title: Read from the right
solutions.idea: Walking backwards, a # tells you up front that the two digits before it belong together.

followups: Write the encoder too. Could a different marker scheme avoid look-ahead entirely?
Without the # marks, count how many messages a digit string could decode to.
lcTitle: Decrypt String from Alphabet to Integer Mapping
